summary: This quickstart walks a developer from a checked-in extension example to a deterministic package artifact, a narrow permission review, and a host-rendered result. It uses a fresh temporary folder, validates the package for one host, and compares two pack outputs. The example asks for optional library metadata access and a required panel operation, showing how denial differs from install failure. The page explains the typed SDK bridge, preview/apply behavior, update and revoke semantics, host availability, and troubleshooting. Desktop and Browser command menus pass staged or active refs separately from guest input, with a 16-ref limit; Terminal has no current-piece selector, so commands must use explicit resource selectors supported by the operation. Three more examples cover draft review, scene events, and prompt contributions.

sections.title: 1. Copy a working example into a clean folder
sections.summary: The exercise starts from the checked-in character-audit example and copies its manifest and entry into a uniquely named temporary directory. It runs the host-aware package check, packs the same source twice, and compares artifact hashes to confirm deterministic output. Both commands validate and bundle without evaluating the entry file. The entry has a bounded UTF-8 size, and import rules restrict dependencies to package-local paths or the generated SDK. The temporary directory is deliberately unique so the workflow does not overwrite an existing fixture or repository file.

sections.title: 2. Review one optional permission and install
sections.summary: The install walkthrough asks the developer to review the package identity and each operation request in Settings. `ui.panel.set` is needed to show the command result, while `content.list` is an optional library-wide metadata grant for character IDs, kinds, and names. The example does not request bodies, prompts, descriptions, or media. The first run denies the optional grant and demonstrates an actionable denial in the panel. A second permission review grants the scope, after which the same command lists bounded character names without changing library content.

sections.title: 3. How the command and panel use the SDK
sections.summary: The SDK example imports `bunzai` from the generated package and defines a command handler with `bunzai.extension.define`. Its typed operation methods are wrappers over one broker bridge, rather than direct host callbacks. The command requests only the declared character metadata fields, then sends a value-only panel descriptor to the host. The manifest declares both operation permissions and the command and panel contribution IDs. The host validates the declared panel and draws it; extension code cannot return HTML, handler source, or permission controls. The broker checks grants at invocation time.

sections.title: 4. Update, disable, and revoke
sections.summary: Updates require a new package review when the artifact bytes change. The walkthrough recommends writing the updated package to a new file, checking its identity and digest, and reapproving only operation requests that remain acceptable. Disabling stops activation while preserving the installed package. Revoking removes grants and stops package-owned panels and actions. Removing the extension and its data also deletes its private settings and activity records, but it does not delete library content. These distinctions help developers document expected recovery behavior without implying that an old approval transfers to new bytes.

sections.title: Preview and apply for content edits
sections.summary: Content mutation is staged as a preview or draft before persistence. The extension inspects the host's exact before-and-after review, then calls the corresponding apply operation with the expected revision and preview fingerprint. A preview alone does not save a change. Resource scope remains explicit: a grant for selected IDs covers those targets, while a library-wide grant is broader and needs deliberate review. The workflow separates proposed content from committed content and makes stale revisions visible instead of silently merging concurrent edits.

sections.title: Host availability
sections.summary: The generated catalog and host-aware check report which operations have concrete adapters on desktop, browser, and terminal. SDK types describe the source catalog, but an installed host determines whether a particular operation is available. Native file selection, network requests, UI gestures, and provider connections have host-specific boundaries. Desktop and Browser command menus attach staged or active refs as separate host context; Terminal has no current-piece selector or `--on` flag, so commands use explicit resource selectors supported by each operation. Naming an operation in a manifest does not make an unsupported host implementation appear. Developers should run `extensions:check` against the actual target host and keep example claims aligned with the adapters that have been exercised.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.summary: The troubleshooting list maps common failures to specific checks: confirm operation IDs in the generated reference, validate the manifest and declared file paths, enable an installed package, and match contribution IDs to defined handlers. For access denial, inspect the exact operation, resources, and fields before granting anything. If an update stops working, review its new bytes and digest. Host-specific failures should be checked on that host rather than inferred from another composition. The guide links to generated API and SDK references for strict schemas and error codes.

sections.title: More checked workflows
sections.summary: Three checked examples extend the basic audit workflow. The draft-writer example stages a two-field character change and applies the reviewed fingerprint under an exact resource grant. The event-panel example subscribes to the safe `scene.opened` summary and displays it through the bounded panel API. The prompt-contributor example adds a manifest-declared candidate to one scene's system prompt stage during host preview. Each source can be copied to a temporary directory, checked for its target host, and packed. Manifest requirements describe requested scope but do not silently grant a library-wide resource selector.
